From factorial divergence to convergent coefficients

Mellin connections and inverse reconstruction in the Lieb–Liniger model

Istvan Vona

13 November 2026

Download PDFLaTeX source ZIP Paper + code + data

Abstract

How can a factorially divergent expansion at one end of parameter space encode a convergent expansion at the other? We develop a coefficient-level answer, beginning with the exponential integral and ending with the repulsive Lieb–Liniger integral equation. For Stieltjes transforms, a single meromorphic moment function connects positive-index values to negative-index values, residues and finite parts. The exponential integral makes factorials, reciprocal factorials and harmonic numbers parts of one gamma-function identity. A two-parameter confluent-hypergeometric family explains Airy connection formulas and logarithmic resonance; an exactly solvable Riccati equation shows how nonlinearity and independent trans-series data modify the picture. We then prove holomorphy of the Love–Lieb resolvent on a slit parameter plane, obtain a convergent conformal expansion reaching every positive coupling, and derive the algebraic structure of Lang’s regrouped strong-coupling series. First differences of the conformal coefficients give an explicit Laguerre inverse-Laplace transform. Exponentials become translated supports, allowing recursive recovery of sector germs under stated resurgent continuation assumptions. The exact transform, a finite-data smoothing bound, the conditional sector theorem and numerical evidence are kept logically separate. A recomputed 4,000-coefficient dataset detects five action thresholds and estimates the first logarithmic strength within 1.9%; it does not yet resolve higher fluctuation coefficients. The resulting framework identifies both the connection mechanism and the global information that a local asymptotic series alone can omit.

Keywords: asymptotic expansions; resurgence; Mellin transforms; coefficient interpolation; Laplace inversion; Lieb–Liniger model.

1 The connection problem and the meaning of a coefficient map#

A single exact function can have a divergent expansion at infinity and a convergent expansion at the origin. The disparity is especially striking when one sequence grows like n! while another contains 1/n!. This is not a contradiction: the expansions probe different parts of the same analytic object. The useful question is more demanding than whether analytic continuation connects them:

Which explicit operations on one coefficient sequence recover the other, including logarithms, exponential sectors and their amplitudes?

There are three distinct answers, which should not be conflated. A finite triangular map computes a transformed coefficient from finitely many input coefficients. An infinite-data connection reconstructs analytic continuation or a transform from the complete sequence. A large-order correspondence identifies the asymptotic signature of a sector in that sequence. The first is algebraic, the second global, and the third asymptotic. None automatically provides a well-conditioned algorithm from a finite noisy prefix.

Throughout, “convergent expansion” means convergence in its stated variable. A convergent power–log expansion is not a Taylor series, and convergence in a conformal coordinate does not imply convergence of the original coupling series everywhere. In the elementary examples, z→∞ is the asymptotic endpoint. In Lieb–Liniger, weak physical coupling is the asymptotic endpoint; the auxiliary variable B=1/α or w plays the role of large z.

1.1 The two mechanisms#

The first mechanism is a Mellin connection. If

G⁢(z)=∫0∞ρ⁢(t)z+t⁢dt,ϕ⁢(v)=∫0∞tv⁢ρ⁢(t)⁢dt, (1.1)

then the asymptotic coefficients of G are (−1)n⁢ϕ⁢(n). The local coefficients at zero are obtained from the continuation of ϕ to negative indices. Regular values give powers, poles give logarithms, and finite parts fix the accompanying regular terms. This is a consequence of Mellin inversion and, in a broader class, of Ramanujan’s master theorem [1, 2].

The second mechanism is an inverse transform. For a function holomorphic in a disk, its Taylor coefficients can be converted into the Laguerre coefficients of a causal inverse-Laplace kernel. The elementary identity

ℒ⁢[𝟏t>A⁢g⁢(t−A)]⁢(w)=e−A⁢w⁢ℒ⁢[g]⁢(w) (1.2)

turns exponentially small sectors into finite-location structure. This is classical Laplace inversion [3]; its particular application to conformal Love–Lieb coefficients supplies the inverse construction developed below.

The relation between global holomorphy and weak/strong expansions has precedents, including the analysis of finite-dimensional integrals in Ref. [4]. The present treatment does not claim a new general Mellin theorem or a new general Laguerre inversion theorem. Its purpose is to put the coefficient maps, their assumptions and their failure modes into one derivation, and to apply them to the specific integral equation.

1.2 Results and their logical status#

The progression is deliberately elementary to nontrivial. Sections 2–6 give exact-function laboratories. Sections 7–9 establish the strong-origin analytic continuation and explain the weak boundary. Sections 10 and 11 give the inverse map and its conditional sector decomposition. Section 12 reports the actual finite-data tests.

2 The exponential integral: one coefficient function, two endpoints#

2.1 Fixing the Borel convention#

For an inverse-power series beginning at z−1, use

G⁢(z)∼∑n≥0an⁢z−n−1,G^⁢(p)=∑n≥0ann!⁢pn,G⁢(z)=∫0∞e−z⁢p⁢G^⁢(p)⁢dp. (2.1)

The last equality requires a specified continuation and Laplace contour; it is not the definition of every function with the displayed asymptotic series. For a series beginning at z0, the corresponding shifted sum is z⁢ℒ⁢[G^]⁢(z).

The alternating factorial series is represented by

G⁢(z)=ez⁢E1⁢(z)=∫0∞e−z⁢p1+p⁢dp=∫0∞e−tz+t⁢dt,ℜ⁡z>0. (2.2)

The second representation follows by writing (1+p)−1=∫0∞e−(1+p)⁢t⁢dt and exchanging integrals. Expanding at p=0 gives

G⁢(z)∼∑n≥0(−1)n⁢n!zn+1. (2.3)

Thus z⁢G⁢(z), with x=1/z, realizes the original formal series ∑(−1)n⁢n!⁢xn. The factorial is simply the Laplace integral of pn.

At the other endpoint, the standard convergent representation of E1 gives [5]

G⁢(z)=∑n≥0znn!⁢(Hn−γE−log⁡z),H0=0. (2.4)

Here a branch of log⁡z is fixed; the two coefficient functions multiplying 1 and log⁡z are entire. Why do the very different sequences in equations (2.3) and (2.4) belong together?

2.2 Factorials are values; reciprocal factorials are residues#

The Stieltjes density in equation (2.2) is ρ⁢(t)=e−t. Its moment function is

ϕ⁢(v)=∫0∞tv⁢e−t⁢dt=Γ⁢(v+1). (2.5)

At positive indices, ϕ⁢(n)=n!. At v=−n−1, the Laurent expansion is

ϕ⁢(v)=(−1)nn!⁢[1v+n+1+Hn−γE+O⁢(v+n+1)]. (2.6)

The residues are reciprocal factorials, and the finite parts contain harmonic numbers. The Mellin identity

ℳ⁢G⁢(s)=πsin⁡π⁢s⁢ϕ⁢(s−1)=π⁢Γ⁢(s)sin⁡π⁢s,0<ℜ⁡s<1, (2.7)

turns these Laurent coefficients directly into equation (2.4). At s=−n, the two factors each have a simple pole. Multiplication by z−s makes their double pole produce −zn⁢log⁡z.

This is the first coefficient dictionary:

n!=Γ(n+1),(−1)nn!=Resv=−n−1Γ(v+1),(−1)n⁢(Hn−γE)n!=FPv=−n−1Γ(v+1). (2.8)

There is no factorial “turning into” an inverse factorial by a termwise substitution in z. The two sequences sample different analytic data of the same function of the coefficient index.

2.3 The nonalternating series and independent exponentially small data#

The companion function

G+⁢(z)=PV⁢∫0∞e−z⁢p1−p⁢dp=e−z⁢Ei⁡(z)∼∑n≥0n!zn+1 (2.9)

has a Borel pole on the integration ray. Upper and lower contour indentations give G+±i⁢π⁢e−z, respectively, with “upper” referring to a path that passes above p=1. Their difference is 2⁢π⁢ie−z. The small-z expansion is

G+⁢(z)+C⁢e−z=∑n≥0(−1)n⁢znn!⁢(γE+log⁡z−Hn+C). (2.10)

Every C gives the same algebraic asymptotic expansion at positive infinity. The equation G+′+G+=1/z allows precisely this homogeneous addition. A boundary condition or a summation convention fixes it. Thus an exponentially small parameter at one endpoint becomes an ordinary local coefficient at the other.

2.4 Incomplete gamma: two sectors collide to make a logarithm#

For q>0, define

Iq⁢(z)=∫0∞e−z⁢p(1+p)q⁢dp=ez⁢zq−1⁢Γ⁢(1−q,z),ϕq⁢(v)=Γ⁢(q+v)Γ⁢(q). (2.11)

The moment representation uses ρq⁢(t)=tq−1⁢e−t/Γ⁢(q), and

Iq⁢(z)∼∑n≥0(−1)n⁢(q)n⁢z−n−1. (2.12)

For noninteger q, the exact local decomposition is

Iq(z)=Γ(1−q)zq−1ez+∑n≥0zn(q−1)⁢(2−q)n. (2.13)

It follows either from the incomplete-gamma series [6] or from the residue calculation below. The two power-series factors converge for every finite z. The regular coefficients are the continued negative moments

(−1)n⁢ϕq⁢(−n−1)=1(q−1)⁢(2−q)n. (2.14)

The fractional sector comes from the other pole family.

Set q=1+ε. Then

Γ⁢(−ε)⁢zε =−ε−1−γE−log⁡z+O⁢(ε), (2.15)
1ε⁢(1−ε)n =1n!⁢(ε−1+Hn+O⁢(ε)). (2.16)

The poles cancel between the two sectors of equation (2.13); their finite remainder is equation (2.4). A logarithm is therefore both a double Mellin pole and the finite remnant of colliding power-law families.

3 The complete Mellin dictionary, and its limitations#

3.1 A local Borel tail is not the whole connection#

Let G=ℒ⁢[B] and define MB⁢(v)=∫0∞pv−1⁢B⁢(p)⁢dp in a nonempty fundamental strip. Exchanging the two convergent integrals gives

ℳG(s)=Γ(s)MB(1−s). (3.1)

The continuation of this product governs the opposite endpoint. A formal large-p term c⁢p−α supplies the singular contribution

c⁢Γ⁢(1−α)⁢zα−1. (3.2)

At integer α, the finite part introduces a logarithm. But this rule alone can omit regular powers of z.

A decisive example is

B0⁢(p)=11+p,B1⁢(p)=11+p+e−p. (3.3)

The two functions have identical inverse-power expansions at positive infinity, while

ℒ⁢[B1]⁢(z)−ℒ⁢[B0]⁢(z)=1z+1. (3.4)

Every regular Taylor coefficient changes. Likewise, applying equation (3.2) to (1+p)−q recovers only the first term of equation (2.13); for q=3/2 it misses the nonzero value I3/2⁢(0)=2.

Proposition 3.1 (Singular terms and regularized moments).

Assume that equation (3.1) admits meromorphic continuation and that the relevant inverse-Mellin contour displacements are justified by bounds on vertical lines and their remainders. If MB is regular at n+1, the gamma pole at s=−n contributes

(−1)nn!⁢MB⁢(n+1)⁢zn. (3.5)

If, instead,

MB⁢(v)=−cnv−n−1+hn+O⁢(v−n−1), (3.6)

the contribution is

(−1)n⁢znn!⁢[hn+cn⁢(Hn−γE−log⁡z)]. (3.7)

These statements describe the residues; they do not by themselves prove convergence of the resulting local expansion.

Proof.

Put s=−n+ε. Then MB⁢(1−s)=cn/ε+hn+O⁢(ε), while Γ⁢(s)=(−1)n⁢[n!⁢ε]−1⁢[1+(Hn−γE)⁢ε+⋯] and z−s=zn⁢(1−ε⁢log⁡z+⋯). The residue gives equation (3.7). The regular case has only the gamma pole. ∎

The finite parts hn retain global information. For B⁢(p)=(1+p)−1, MB⁢(v)=π/sin⁡π⁢v has zero constant Laurent coefficient at its integers; this special cancellation explains why the abbreviated tail rule succeeds there.

3.2 Continuing the coefficient index#

For a Stieltjes representation equation (1.1), a direct beta integral gives

ℳ⁢G⁢(s)=∫0∞ρ⁢(t)⁢[∫0∞zs−1z+t⁢dz]⁢dt=πsin⁡π⁢s⁢ϕ⁢(s−1). (3.8)

The interchange is first made where absolutely convergent; subsequent use relies on continuation. The resulting inverse-Mellin integral is

G⁢(z)=12⁢π⁢i⁢∫c−i⁢∞c+i⁢∞πsin⁡π⁢s⁢ϕ⁢(s−1)⁢z−s⁢ds. (3.9)
Proposition 3.2 (Coefficient-index dictionary).

Under the contour hypotheses of proposition 3.1, the large-z coefficients are (−1)n⁢ϕ⁢(n). If ϕ is regular at −n−1, its ordinary local contribution is

[zn]reg⁢G=(−1)n⁢ϕ⁢(−n−1). (3.10)

If

ϕ⁢(v)=rnv+n+1+dn+O⁢(v+n+1), (3.11)

its contribution is

(−1)nzn(dn−rnlogz). (3.12)

Other poles of ϕ⁢(s−1) yield fractional powers; higher pole multiplicities yield higher powers of log⁡z.

Proof.

At s=−n+ε, π/sin⁡π⁢s=(−1)n⁢(ε−1+O⁢(ε)). In particular this factor has no constant Laurent term. Multiplying by ϕ⁢(s−1)⁢z−s proves the local formulas. The right-hand poles at s=n+1 give the large-z coefficients, with the reversed contour orientation accounting for the sign. ∎

The formula can hold without a positive density. If

B⁢(p)=∑n≥0(−1)n⁢ϕ⁢(n)n!⁢pn (3.13)

and the analyticity and growth assumptions of Ramanujan’s master theorem apply, then MB⁢(s)=Γ⁢(s)⁢ϕ⁢(−s) and equation (3.8) follows [2]. Positivity is a helpful sufficient structure, not a universal requirement.

3.3 Interpolation is global data, not a free substitution#

Knowing ϕ⁢(n) for all n≥0 does not select an arbitrary meromorphic interpolation uniquely. The exact ambiguity

ϕ~⁢(v)=Γ⁢(v+1)+CΓ⁢(−v) (3.14)

has the same positive-index values as Γ⁢(v+1), since 1/Γ⁢(−n)=0. Nevertheless,

πsin⁡π⁢s⁢CΓ⁢(1−s)=C⁢Γ⁢(s) (3.15)

adds C⁢e−z to the inverse Mellin transform. Thus a term invisible at every nonnegative coefficient index can encode an entire exponentially small function. It does not satisfy the same moment/growth hypotheses as the selected Stieltjes interpolation. Nor is the added function asserted to solve the original exponential-integral differential equation.

This example makes the role of admissibility concrete. A density, a differential equation with boundary conditions, or a suitable uniqueness theorem for the interpolation fixes the missing information. Positive moment problems with a finite exponential moment are determinate: their moment generating functions are analytic near zero and are fixed by all their derivatives there. Without such a class, the formal asymptotic sequence does not determine all exponentially small additions.

3.4 The general rule for logarithms and convergence#

The reliable logarithm rule is multiplicity, not integrality:

A pole of order r in the full Mellin integrand produces(logz)r−1 at highest degree. (3.16)

Zeros in other factors may cancel a pole. A noninteger power already accompanied by log⁡p can produce a logarithm without any integer resonance.

Nor does Borel summability at infinity guarantee a convergent expansion at zero. For example, B⁢(p)=e−1+p is analytic at p=0 and decreases faster than every power on the positive ray, but the formal derivatives of G=ℒ⁢[B] at zero give

[zn]formal⁢G=(−1)nn!⁢∫0∞pn⁢e−1+p⁢dp∼2⁢(−1)n⁢Γ⁢(2⁢n+2)n!. (3.17)

The local series has zero radius. Convergence in the examples below follows from their additional analytic structure, not from the gamma kernel alone.

4 Airy and a master family of exact connection formulas#

4.1 One Mellin–Barnes integral contains both expansions#

For μ,ν>0, define

Φμ,ν⁢(w)=wμ⁢U⁢(μ,1+μ−ν,w). (4.1)

The standard large-argument expansion of U [7] becomes

Φμ,ν⁢(w)∼∑n≥0(−1)n⁢(μ)n⁢(ν)nn!⁢wn,Φ^⁢(p)=F12⁢(μ,ν;1;−p). (4.2)

The shifted Borel sum is w⁢ℒ⁢[Φ^]⁢(w). The interpolation associated with Φ/w is

ϕμ,ν⁢(v)=Γ⁢(μ+v)⁢Γ⁢(ν+v)Γ⁢(μ)⁢Γ⁢(ν)⁢Γ⁢(1+v). (4.3)

An equivalent and especially transparent connection is

Φμ,ν(w)=12⁢π⁢i⁢Γ⁢(μ)⁢Γ⁢(ν)∫c−i⁢∞c+i⁢∞Γ(−s)Γ(μ+s)Γ(ν+s)w−sds, (4.4)

where −min⁡(μ,ν)<c<0 and initially w>0. Moving the contour right encounters the poles of Γ⁢(−s) at 0,1,2,… and gives the factorial expansion. Moving left encounters s=−μ−n and s=−ν−n and gives, for μ−ν∉ℤ,

Φμ,ν⁢(w)= Γ⁢(ν−μ)Γ⁢(ν)⁢wμ⁢F11⁢(μ;1+μ−ν;w)
+Γ⁢(μ−ν)Γ⁢(μ)⁢wν⁢F11⁢(ν;1+ν−μ;w). (4.5)

This is Kummer’s connection formula, interpreted as a coefficient map. In particular Φ1,q⁢(w)=w⁢Iq⁢(w), so the incomplete-gamma example is already part of this family.

The coefficient ratios make the growth contrast immediate. At infinity the ratio is

−(n+μ)⁢(n+ν)n+1∼−n, (4.6)

whereas in the first local tower it is

n+μ(n+1+μ−ν)⁢(n+1)∼1n. (4.7)

Factorial growth and inverse-factorial decay are generated by different residues of one integral, not by unrelated formulas.

When μ=ν, the two left families coalesce. Taking the limit in equation (4.5) yields

Φμ,μ⁢(w)=wμΓ⁢(μ)⁢∑n≥0(μ)n⁢wn(n!)2⁢[−log⁡w+2⁢ψ⁢(n+1)−ψ⁢(μ+n)]. (4.8)

For μ=1/2, the exponent is noninteger but there is still a logarithm. This is why the pole-multiplicity rule is preferable to an “integer exponent” rule.

4.2 The Airy specialization#

Set

ξ=23⁢x3/2,w=2⁢ξ,𝒜⁢(ξ)=2⁢π⁢x1/4⁢eξ⁢Ai⁡(x). (4.9)

The Airy–Bessel and Bessel–Kummer identities [8, 7] give

𝒜⁢(ξ)=2⁢ξπ⁢eξ⁢K1/3⁢(ξ)=Φ1/6,5/6⁢(2⁢ξ). (4.10)

Consequently,

𝒜⁢(ξ)∼∑n≥0(−1)n⁢(1/6)n⁢(5/6)n2n⁢n!⁢ξn,B𝒜⁢(p)=F12⁢(16,56;1;−p2). (4.11)

The nearest finite Borel singularity is at p=−2. It controls factorial large order at infinity. The large-p behavior, by contrast, contains the two power families p−1/6−n and p−5/6−n; these control the opposite endpoint.

For either λ=1/6 or 5/6, the corresponding Borel tower is

Dλ⁢p−λ⁢∑n≥0(−2)n⁢(λ)n2(2⁢λ)n⁢n!⁢p−n,Dλ=2λ⁢Γ⁢(1−2⁢λ)Γ⁢(1−λ)2. (4.12)

Using the shifted kernel p−λ−n↦Γ⁢(1−λ−n)⁢ξλ+n and

Γ⁢(1−λ−n)=(−1)n⁢Γ⁢(1−λ)(λ)n (4.13)

turns its coefficient into

Dλ⁢Γ⁢(1−λ)⁢2n⁢(λ)n(2⁢λ)n⁢n!⁢ξλ+n. (4.14)

One rising factorial cancels, leaving a convergent hypergeometric tower. This is an explicit coefficient-by-coefficient calculation once the Borel connection at infinity has been made.

The exact local answer can be written

𝒜⁢(ξ)= C0ξ1/6eξF10(;23;ξ24)+C1ξ5/6eξF10(;43;ξ24), (4.15)
C0= 2−1/6⁢Γ⁢(1/3)π,C1=−3 2−5/6⁢Γ⁢(2/3)π. (4.16)

Undoing the normalization gives the entire Taylor expansion

Ai⁡(x)=F10(;2/3;x3/9)32/3⁢Γ⁢(2/3)−xF10(;4/3;x3/9)31/3⁢Γ⁢(1/3). (4.17)

The fractional powers in equation (4.15) arise from the ramified coordinate and normalization, not from a singularity of Ai at zero.

4.3 Why the abbreviated tail rule happens to be complete here#

There is no missing integer-power sector because

ϕ1/6,5/6⁢(−n−1)=0(n≥0). (4.18)

The numerator gamma functions in equation (4.3) are finite at these points, while the reciprocal denominator gamma function vanishes. These are exactly the regularized negative moments that could have supplied additional ordinary powers. Their vanishing is a global property of this Borel function.

The normalized differential equation provides the same local diagnosis:

𝒜′′−2⁢𝒜′+536⁢ξ2⁢𝒜=0. (4.19)

Its indicial roots are 1/6 and 5/6, with noninteger difference, so no resonant logarithm is required.

Finally, the master family has, for μ>0 and 0<ν<1, the positive density

ρμ,ν⁢(t)=tμ−1⁢e−tΓ⁢(μ)⁢Γ⁢(ν)⁢U⁢(1−ν,1+μ−ν,t),Φμ,ν⁢(w)w=∫0∞ρμ,ν⁢(t)w+t⁢dt. (4.20)

For Airy this becomes the self-representation

Φ1/6,5/6⁢(w)w=12⁢π⁢∫0∞e−t⁢Φ1/6,5/6⁢(t)t⁢(w+t)⁢dt. (4.21)

Thus its factorial coefficients are also positive moments of a density containing the same normalized Airy function. A derivation is given in appendix A.

5 Riccati: nonlinearity, logarithms and two different large-parameter branches#

Consider

f′⁢(z)+f⁢(z)−f⁢(z)2+1z=0. (5.1)

The substitution f=−u′/u yields u′′+u′−u/z=0. Independent solutions are u1=z and u2=z⁢E1⁢(z)−e−z, so

fc⁢(z)=c+E1⁢(z)e−z−z⁢(c+E1⁢(z)),c∈ℂ, (5.2)

with the exceptional solution f=−1/z at c=∞. This elementary linearization makes the nonlinear connection problem exact.

5.1 The factorial branch as a moment problem#

The distinguished branch tending to 1 along the positive axis is f∗=f0. With G=ez⁢E1⁢(z),

f∗⁢(z)=G⁢(z)1−z⁢G⁢(z)∼1+1z−2z2+8z3−44z4+296z5−⋯. (5.3)

The algebraic transformation of G is already an exact computational coefficient map. More revealingly,

f∗(z)−1=∫0∞ρR⁢(t)z+tdt,ρR(t)=e−t(1−t⁢e−t⁢Ei⁡(t))2+π2⁢t2⁢e−2⁢t. (5.4)

To verify it, observe that 1−z⁢G⁢(z)=∫0∞t⁢e−t/(z+t)⁢dt has no zeros off the negative cut: its imaginary part has strict sign opposite to ℑ⁡z, and it is positive for z>0. On the upper bank, G⁢(−t+i0)=−e−t⁢(Ei⁡(t)+i⁢π). Taking the imaginary part of G/(1+t⁢G) gives the density in equation (5.4); Cauchy’s formula then reconstructs f∗−1. Details of the endpoint estimates are in appendix A.

Writing

f∗⁢(z)=1+∑n≥0(−1)n⁢μn⁢z−n−1, (5.5)

we obtain

μn=∫0∞tn⁢ρR⁢(t)⁢dt,(μ0,μ1,…)=(1,2,8,44,296,2312,…). (5.6)

The Borel equation is particularly simple. If h=ℬ⁢[f∗−1], then

(1+p)⁢h⁢(p)+(h∗h)⁢(p)=1,h⁢(p)=∫0∞e−p⁢t⁢ρR⁢(t)⁢dt. (5.7)

Equating coefficients gives a positive recurrence,

μ0=1,μn=n⁢μn−1+∑j=0n−1μj⁢μn−1−j. (5.8)

Nonlinearity becomes convolution, while the spectral density makes the moment interpretation survive.

The two density endpoints explain the two expansions:

ρR⁢(t) =t2⁢e−t⁢(1−4t+O⁢(t−2)), t→∞, (5.9)
ρR⁢(t) =1+t⁢(2⁢log⁡t+2⁢γE−1)+O⁢(t2⁢log2⁡t), t↓0. (5.10)

The first yields

μn=Γ⁢(n+3)⁢(1−4n+2+O⁢(n−2)). (5.11)

The second yields logarithms at the origin and the large-p Borel tail

h⁢(p)=1p+1−2⁢log⁡pp2+O⁢(log2⁡pp3). (5.12)

5.2 A convergent local power–log expansion#

Set L=c−γE−log⁡z and g⁢(z)=∑m≥1(−1)m+1⁢zm/(m⁢m!). Then

fc⁢(z)=L+g⁢(z)e−z−z⁢(L+g⁢(z))=∑n≥0pn⁢(L)⁢zn, (5.13)

where

p0⁢(L) =L, (5.14)
p1⁢(L) =L2+L+1, (5.15)
p2⁢(L) =L3+2⁢L2+52⁢L+34. (5.16)

Substitution in the differential equation gives the polynomial recurrence

pn+1′⁢(L)−(n+1)⁢pn+1⁢(L)=pn⁢(L)−∑j=0npj⁢(L)⁢pn−j⁢(L). (5.17)

It determines a unique polynomial of degree n+2. Convergence near zero on any fixed logarithmic sector follows from the exact quotient: z⁢log⁡z→0, so its denominator can be expanded geometrically. Unlike the linear special functions, the nonlinear quotient can have poles away from zero. Its local coefficients need not have global inverse-factorial decay. What survives is the exact coefficient connection, not a universal rate of local coefficient decay.

5.3 The trans-series parameter belongs to the other asymptotic branch#

For c≠0, put σ=1/c and

Q⁢(z)=e−zz−E1⁢(z)=Γ⁢(−1,z)∼e−zz2⁢∑n≥0(−1)n⁢(n+1)!⁢z−n. (5.18)

An exact rearrangement gives

fc(z)=−1z−σ⁢e−zz2⁢[1−σ⁢Q⁢(z)]. (5.19)

Expanding the denominator generates all sectors e−k⁢z with factorial fluctuation series. Every finite σ has the algebraic expansion −1/z, whereas c=0 gives the distinct factorial branch f∗∼1+1/z+⋯.

This distinction is important. The parameter σ is not an arbitrary exponentially small deformation of f∗ on the positive ray. Linearization gives δ⁢f′∼δ⁢f around f∗, but δ⁢f′∼−(1+2/z)⁢δ⁢f around −1/z. The decaying deformation belongs to the latter branch. At the origin the same datum is the ordinary integration constant c=1/σ in L.

Counterclockwise continuation around zero gives E1↦E1−2⁢π⁢i, hence

c↦c−2⁢π⁢i,σ↦σ1−2⁢π⁢i⁢σ. (5.20)

This is an exact global monodromy relation. Splitting it into individual Stokes transformations requires the relevant sector conventions.

6 A full-line integral equation with an exact zeta–Bernoulli bridge#

Before introducing interval boundaries, consider the Poisson convolution equation

u−Pα∗u=f,Pα⁢(x)=απ⁢(α2+x2),f^⁢(k)=|k|⁢e−|k|,α>0. (6.1)

Use f^⁢(k)=∫ℝe−i⁢k⁢x⁢f⁢(x)⁢dx. The source is f⁢(x)=(1−x2)/[π⁢(1+x2)2], and Fourier diagonalization gives

u^⁢(k)=|k|⁢e−|k|1−e−α⁢|k|. (6.2)

For H⁢(α)=π⁢u⁢(0),

H⁢(α)=∫0∞k⁢e−k1−e−α⁢k⁢dk=∑m≥01(1+m⁢α)2=α−2⁢ψ1⁢(1/α). (6.3)

The trigamma representation is standard [9]; the following connection follows directly from the integral equation.

At large α, expanding each summand for m≥1 gives the convergent series

H⁢(α)=1+∑n≥0(−1)n⁢(n+1)⁢ζ⁢(n+2)⁢α−n−2,|α|>1. (6.4)

At small α,

H⁢(α)∼1α+12+∑n≥1B2⁢n⁢α2⁢n−1=1α+12+α6−α330+⋯. (6.5)

The latter is factorially divergent. Both expansions are residues of the single Mellin transform

∫0∞αs−1[H(α)−1]dα=Γ(s)Γ(2−s)ζ(s),1<ℜs<2. (6.6)

Indeed, integrate (1+m⁢α)−2, scale by m, and sum m−s. The right poles at s=2,3,… give equation (6.4). The left poles give equation (6.5); the functional values ζ⁢(1−2⁢n)=−B2⁢n/(2⁢n) supply Bernoulli numbers, and the trivial zeros of zeta cancel the negative even gamma poles. There are no multiple poles, hence no logarithms.

This example also warns against importing a Stokes geometry merely because the kernel looks similar. Writing z=1/α gives

H⁢(α)=z2⁢∫0∞e−z⁢t⁢t1−e−t⁢dt. (6.7)

Its finite Borel singularities lie at t=±2⁢π⁢i,±4⁢π⁢i,…. They are not the positive real actions of the finite-interval Lieb–Liniger problem. The interval boundary is an essential part of that difference.

7 Lieb–Liniger: a convergent coordinate for the full repulsive branch#

7.1 Integral equation and physical normalization#

The repulsive Lieb–Liniger gas has contact interaction strength c>0, particle density n, and physical coupling γ=c/n. In the thermodynamic ground state, the rapidities occupy [−Q,Q]. Rescaling k=Q⁢x and putting α=c/Q gives the Love–Lieb equation [10, 11]

u⁢(x;α)−1π⁢∫−11α⁢u⁢(y;α)α2+(x−y)2⁢dy=1,−1≤x≤1. (7.1)

We use

Ij⁢(α)=∫−11xj⁢u⁢(x;α)⁢dx,γ=2⁢π⁢αI0,e(γ)=4⁢π2⁢I2I03. (7.2)

Here E0/N=(ℏ2⁢n2/2⁢m)⁢e⁢(γ) and u⁢(x)=2⁢π⁢ρ⁢(Q⁢x). Strong coupling means α→∞; weak coupling means α→0+. The moment problem is linear, although eliminating α to obtain e⁢(γ) is nonlinear.

At large γ the first terms are

e⁢(γ)=π23⁢[1−4γ+12γ2+(−32+32⁢π215)⁢γ−3+⋯]. (7.3)

A systematic perturbative construction and the weak-coupling trans-series are available in Refs. [12, 14]; our input below is instead the strong-origin coefficient germ.

7.2 Holomorphy of the resolvent on a slit plane#

Let Kα be the integral operator in equation (7.1) on ℋ=L2⁢[−1,1].

Theorem 7.1 (Slit-plane resolvent).

The family Tα=(I−Kα)−1 is holomorphic on

Ω=ℂ^∖i⁢[−2,2], (7.4)

including α=∞. For every nonzero g∈ℋ,

ℜ⁡⟨g,Tα⁢g⟩>0. (7.5)

In particular, I0 has positive real part and never vanishes on Ω.

Proof.

The kernel is continuous on the square and holomorphic in α off the slit, so Kα is a holomorphic compact-operator family. For ℜ⁡α>0, zero extension to the line and restriction back to the interval give

Kα=P⁢e−α⁢|D|⁢P. (7.6)

For each nonzero v∈ℋ, Plancherel’s theorem implies

∥Kα⁢v∥≤∥e−α⁢|D|⁢v∥<∥v∥. (7.7)

The inequality is strict because the Fourier multiplier has modulus strictly below one except at the measure-zero set k=0. A nonzero compact operator attains its norm; hence ∥Kα∥<1. For ℜ⁡α<0, use Kα=−K−α. For α=i⁢β with |β|>2, the kernel is imaginary and symmetric, so Kα is skew-adjoint and I−Kα is invertible. Local analytic inversion proves holomorphy, and Kα→0 in norm at infinity.

If u=Tα⁢g, taking real parts in g=(I−Kα)⁢u gives

ℜ⁡⟨g,u⟩=∥u∥2−ℜ⁡⟨u,Kα⁢u⟩>0. (7.8)

Use the strict contraction off the imaginary axis and skew-adjointness on its remaining part. Choosing g=1 yields the claim about I0. ∎

The theorem is about the auxiliary kernel parameter. It does not assert that e is single-valued on the entire complex γ plane: the map α↦γ can have critical points.

7.3 A disk containing the whole positive axis#

Introduce

a=α2+4−α2,α=1a−a, (7.9)

with the branch a∼1/α at infinity. The inverse Joukowski map identifies Ω with |a|<1; a=0 is strong coupling and a→1− is weak coupling. It follows that

u⁢(x;α⁢(a))=∑n≥0vn⁢(x)⁢an,Mj⁢(a):=Ij⁢(α⁢(a))=∑n≥0bn(j)⁢an (7.10)

converge locally uniformly in the disk, the first in L2. Since I0≠0, the energy composed with a is holomorphic there too. Every positive coupling is reached parametrically.

If the original expansion is u=∑j≥0uj⁢α−j, then

v0=u0=1,vN=∑k=0⌊(N−1)/2⌋(N−k−1k)uN−2⁢k(N≥1). (7.11)

This follows from α−1=a/(1−a2). It is a finite triangular map and contains no weak-coupling input. The first terms are v1=u1, v2=u2, v3=u3+u1 and v4=u4+2⁢u2.

7.4 Uniform coefficient bounds#

The positive-real-part property supplies more than holomorphy.

Corollary 7.2 (Bounded conformal moment coefficients).

For each integer j≥0, the coefficients in equation (7.10) obey

|bn(j)|≤Bj:=2+22⁢j+1(n≥0). (7.12)

In particular |bn(0)|≤4 and |bn(2)|≤12/5.

Proof.

For fixed real g, the function Fg⁢(a)=⟨g,Tα⁢(a)⁢g⟩ has positive real part and Fg⁢(0)=∥g∥2. Its nonconstant Taylor coefficients have modulus at most 2⁢∥g∥2, by integrating the nonnegative function ℜ⁡Fg⁢(r⁢ei⁢θ) against Fourier modes and sending r↑1. The operator is symmetric under transpose, so

Mj⁢(a)=14⁢{F1+xj⁢(a)−F1−xj⁢(a)}. (7.13)

The bound is therefore 12⁢(∥1+xj∥2+∥1−xj∥2)=2+2/(2⁢j+1) for n≥1; the constant coefficient also satisfies it. Odd moments vanish by parity. ∎

These bounds will provide an explicit error estimate for a smoothed inverse transform. They do not imply that the first differences are square summable or that pointwise derivatives of the unsmoothed inverse are stable.

7.5 The energy coefficients alone are sufficient input#

Let x=1/γ and E⁢(x)=e⁢(1/x)=∑n≥0en⁢xn, with e0=π2/3. The exact Fermi-endpoint identity reviewed in Ref. [15, Sec. 5.3] is, in our notation,

d⁢Bd⁢γ=−12⁢d2d⁢γ2⁢(e⁢(γ)γ2),B=Qc=1α,B⁢(∞)=0. (7.14)

The positive root is selected by B∼π/γ. In the inverse coupling,

Bx=3⁢E+3⁢x⁢E′+12⁢x2⁢E′′. (7.15)

Writing Bx=∑sn⁢xn gives

s0=π,sn=12⁢(n+2)⁢(n+3)⁢en−∑j=1n−1sj⁢sn−j2⁢π,B(x)=∑n≥0snn+1xn+1. (7.16)

Revert the series B⁢(x⁢(a))=a/(1−a2). Then

M0(a)=2⁢π⁢(1−a2)ax(a),M2(a)=E⁢(x⁢(a))⁢M0⁢(a)34⁢π2. (7.17)

Each output coefficient uses only finitely many energy coefficients. For example,

B⁢(x) =π⁢x−2⁢π⁢x2+4⁢π⁢x3+(−8⁢π+43⁢π3)⁢x4+⋯, (7.18)
M0⁢(a) =2+4π⁢a+8π2⁢a2+(43⁢π+16π3)⁢a3+⋯. (7.19)

The boundary condition in equation (7.14) is essential: it fixes the integration constant at the convergent endpoint. The high-order computation below uses the faster kernel recurrence, while the energy-only map is checked separately at low orders.

8 Lang’s regrouping: what the denominators actually encode#

Lang identified a strong-coupling organization of the form [13]

e⁢(γ)=π23⁢γ2(γ+2)2+∑n≥1π2⁢n+2⁢γ2(γ+2)3⁢n+2⁢ℰn⁢(γ),deg⁡ℰn=n−1. (8.1)

The following derivation establishes this as an identity of formal strong-coupling series. It does not assume convergence of the infinite block sum.

8.1 Separate the constant kernel before expanding#

Normalize the density by v=u/I0, so ∫−11v=1, and put τ=1/α. Then 1/I0=γ⁢τ/(2⁢π) and the kernel expansion gives

v⁢(x)=τ⁢(γ+2)2⁢π+τπ⁢∑m≥1(−τ2)m⁢(P2⁢m⁢v)⁢(x),P2⁢m⁢v=∫−11(x−y)2⁢m⁢v⁢(y)⁢dy. (8.2)

The +2 is the constant kernel term combined with the normalization. Keeping only this term gives v=1/2, τ=π/(γ+2) and exactly the leading rational block of equation (8.1).

Set

r=(γ+2)−1,q=π2⁢r2,τ=π⁢r⁢T. (8.3)

Treat q as a formal independent variable while constructing the coefficients. Then

v=T2+r⁢∑m≥1(−q)m⁢T2⁢m+1⁢P2⁢m⁢v,∫v=1. (8.4)

Write T=1+∑Tn⁢(r)⁢qn and v=1/2+∑vn⁢(x,r)⁢qn. If Vn is the order-qn contribution of the sum, involving already known lower coefficients, then

Tn=−∫Vn,vn=Vn−12⁢∫Vn. (8.5)

This is a triangular algebraic construction, not a fit to observed coefficients.

Proposition 8.1 (Formal denominator and degree theorem).

The expansion equation (8.1) holds formally, with rational-coefficient polynomials ℰn of degree exactly n−1. Their leading coefficients are

[γn−1]ℰn(γ)=(−1)n+1⁢22⁢n+3(n+2)⁢(2⁢n+1)⁢(2⁢n+3). (8.6)
Proof.

Each nonconstant-kernel insertion in equation (8.4) brings at least one power of q and one power of r. Induction shows that Tn and vn are divisible by r and have degree at most n in r. Therefore

T2⁢∫x2⁢v=13+∑n≥1qn⁢Cn⁢(r),Cn⁢(r)=∑j=1ncn⁢j⁢rj. (8.7)

Since e=γ2⁢τ2⁢∫x2⁢v, factoring the powers of r gives ℰn⁢(γ)=r−n⁢Cn⁢(r)|r=(γ+2)−1 and the stated denominator, with degree at most n−1. The coefficient of r comes from a single insertion. With Dn=P2⁢n⁢(1/2) it is

[r]⁢Cn=(−1)n⁢∫−11(x2−1)⁢Dn⁢(x)⁢dx=(−1)n+1⁢22⁢n+3(n+2)⁢(2⁢n+1)⁢(2⁢n+3). (8.8)

It is nonzero, establishing the exact degree. ∎

The first polynomials are

ℰ1 =3245, (8.9)
ℰ2 =−16⁢(54⁢γ−53)945, (8.10)
ℰ3 =128⁢(180⁢γ2−306⁢γ+103)14175. (8.11)

The supplied symbolic code verifies the construction through n=5.

8.2 Formal reorganization is not a global convergence theorem#

Every finite sum of the displayed rational blocks is O⁢(γ2) at zero, whereas the exact energy is e⁢(γ)∼γ. Any representation of the weak limit by this grouped sum must therefore involve nonuniform infinite summation. The phrase “infinite radius of convergence” used for partial resummation in Ref. [13] cannot be interpreted as an ordinary entire Taylor expansion in γ; each block has a pole at γ=−2.

There are three separate questions: convergence of the original 1/γ germ, convergence of the sum of rational blocks, and convergence of the conformal moment series. Only the third has been proved globally along the positive axis here. The normalization argument explains Lang’s coefficient pattern but does not replace the slit-plane holomorphy argument.

9 The weak boundary: power–logs, exponentials and physical coupling#

9.1 Where the endpoint logarithms enter#

For α→0+, equation (7.6) suggests I−Kα∼α⁢P⁢|D|⁢P, but this is not a uniform operator expansion. Boundary layers matter. The leading bulk density is a semicircle; the first correction is [11, 15]

u⁢(x;α)∼1−x2α+x⁢log⁡1−x1+x+log⁡16⁢πα+12⁢π⁢1−x2. (9.1)

This expression is nonuniform at x=±1. Integrating its displayed terms gives, with ℓ=log⁡(16⁢π/α),

I0=π2⁢α+ℓ−12+o⁢(1),I2=π8⁢α+ℓ4−712+o⁢(1). (9.2)

In physical variables,

γ=4⁢α2⁢[1−απ⁢(ℓ−1)+o⁢(α)],eγ=1−8⁢α3⁢π+o⁢(α)=1−43⁢π⁢γ+o⁢(γ). (9.3)

The logarithms cancel in the second combination. This first cancellation is explicit; it is not an all-order no-log theorem. Logarithmic structure belongs to the observable and the parameterization, not merely to the equation.

In the disk coordinate, the same weak singularity reads

M0⁢(a)=π4⁢(1−a)−12⁢log⁡(1−a)+O⁢(1). (9.4)

These two terms contribute π/4 and 1/(2⁢n) to the large-order conformal coefficients. Other points of the unit circle can contribute additional terms, so this is not a complete global coefficient asymptotic by itself.

9.2 Actions and the prefactor created by changing coupling#

The auxiliary-moment trans-series of Ref. [14] contains the scales

e−4⁢π⁢k⁢B,B=1/α,k≥1. (9.5)

Introduce the Cayley coordinate

w=1+a1−a,B=a1−a2=14⁢(w−1w). (9.6)

Then the exact action conversion is

e−4⁢π⁢k⁢B=e−k⁢π⁢wek⁢π/w. (9.7)

The first factor is a Laplace translation; the second belongs to its fluctuation series. In the disk, the same scale has a flat essential boundary behavior,

e−4⁢π⁢B∼eπ⁢exp⁡[−2⁢π1−a]. (9.8)

A function can therefore be holomorphic throughout the disk with an ordinary convergent Taylor series and still have a nonperturbative boundary structure.

In physical coupling, put g=γ/(2⁢π). The fundamental scale is e−4/g=e−8⁢π/γ. However, equation (9.2) implies

e−8⁢π/γ∼e2(α16⁢π)2e−4⁢π/α∼eπ+264⁢π2(1−a)2exp[−2⁢π1−a]. (9.9)

The power prefactor is not optional: it comes from exponentiating the logarithm in the coupling conversion, and it changes the coefficient envelope. This is a practical reason to reconstruct the auxiliary moments first and eliminate the coupling last.

At the opposite endpoint, a fixed physical sector e−4⁢k/g loses its smallness as g→∞. Expanding a finite number of weak sectors at strong coupling is consequently nonuniform. The inverse construction below works with the full function rather than attempting that invalid termwise interchange.

9.3 Why the simple positive-moment interpolation does not transfer directly#

Set Z=2⁢π/γ and F⁢(Z)=e⁢(γ)/γ. The first weak coefficients are

F⁢(Z)∼1−83⁢Z+2⁢(π2−6)3⁢Z2+⋯. (9.10)

If F⁢(Z)/Z were a positive Stieltjes transform, its first moments would satisfy μ0=1, μ1=8/3, μ2=2⁢(π2−6)/3. But the necessary moment inequality fails:

μ0⁢μ2−μ12=2⁢π23−1009<0. (9.11)

Signed or complex representations and other observables remain possible. What is excluded is this direct positive-density analogue of the elementary examples.

There is still a common Mellin transform,

ℳ⁢(s)=∫0∞Zs−1⁢F⁢(Z)⁢dZ,−2<ℜ⁡s<0, (9.12)

because F⁢(Z)∼Z2/12 at zero and F⁢(Z)→1 at infinity. Its continued poles would encode both endpoint expansions. But no closed gamma-product interpolation for it is derived here. In particular, an exponentially decreasing contribution integrated over Z≥1 is entire in s, so it is invisible to the large-Z pole principal parts. The global conformal germ supplies precisely the information that those principal parts alone do not.

10 From convergent coefficients to an exact inverse-Laplace kernel#

10.1 A forward sector identity is not yet an inverse#

A boundary exponential has an exact coefficient representation. The Laguerre generating function gives

[an](1−a)βexp[−K1−a]=e−KLn(−β−1)(K). (10.1)

For fixed K>0, its leading large-order behavior is

e−K/2⁢Kβ/2+1/4π⁢n−β/2−3/4⁢cos⁡(2⁢K⁢n+β⁢π2+π4), (10.2)

with the usual lower-order corrections [16]. Logarithmic factors are generated by differentiating with respect to β. Thus exponentially small boundary sectors can leave algebraically small, oscillatory contributions to convergent coefficients.

For a specified global function, equation (10.1) is an exact identity. For a merely local boundary trans-series, it is a contribution to coefficient asymptotics after the required analytic hypotheses are checked. Other boundary singularities and continued lower sectors can overlap with it. Reading off frequencies is therefore not a complete inverse reconstruction.

10.2 An exact Laguerre coefficient transform#

Let M⁢(a)=∑n≥0bn⁢an be one of the conformal moments. Put

H⁢(w)=M⁢((w−1)/(w+1))(w+1)2,qn=bn−bn−12,b−1=0. (10.3)

The factor (w+1)−2 smooths the inversion and makes the leading nonperturbative sector begin with w−2.

Theorem 10.1 (Coefficient-to-kernel inverse).

If {qn}∈ℓ2, then

h(t)=e−t∑n≥0qnLn(2t),H(w)=∫0∞e−w⁢th(t)dt,ℜw>0, (10.4)

where the series converges in L2⁢(0,∞) and

∥h−hN∥22=12⁢∑n>N|qn|2. (10.5)

If the qn have at most polynomial growth, the same formula defines a causal distribution and may be evaluated by Abel regularization,

hr⁢(t)=e−t⁢∑n≥0rn⁢qn⁢Ln⁢(2⁢t),r↑1. (10.6)

In particular, corollary 7.2 supplies this distributional inverse unconditionally for the Love–Lieb moments. Pointwise values and local derivatives require additional regularity.

Proof.

The elementary Laplace pair is

∫0∞e−w⁢t⁢e−t⁢Ln⁢(2⁢t)⁢dt=(w−1)n(w+1)n+1=anw+1. (10.7)

Also,

∑n≥0qn⁢an=1−a2⁢M⁢(a)=M⁢(a)w+1. (10.8)

Summing proves the transform identity. The functions e−t⁢Ln⁢(2⁢t) are orthogonal with squared norm 1/2, proving the L2 statements. For polynomially bounded coefficients, pairing the series with smooth rapidly decreasing test functions on the half-line is convergent: their Laguerre coefficients decrease faster than every inverse power, as follows by repeated integration by parts with the Laguerre differential operator. Extension by zero gives a causal distribution. Abel summation gives the same distributional limit, while its Laplace transform converges geometrically for |a|<1. ∎

This is a specialization of classical Laguerre inversion [3]. Its useful feature here is the particularly simple coefficient rule: first differences of the convergent strong-origin coefficients are the Laguerre coefficients of the inverse kernel.

Unlike a perturbative Borel transform, h is constructed from the full physical function. It retains the information in independent one-sided contributions, not only the singularities of the perturbative germ. No weak-coupling values are sampled in constructing it.

10.3 A controlled finite-data statement#

The unsmoothed inverse may be difficult, but a fixed Abel smoothing has an explicit error estimate.

Proposition 10.2 (Truncation and noise bound).

Suppose |bn|≤B for all n, and supplied coefficients b~n satisfy |b~n−bn|≤η for 0≤n≤N. Define h~r,N by the finite version of equation (10.6), using first differences of b~n. For 0<r<1,

∥hr−h~r,N∥2≤B⁢rN+1+η2⁢(1−r2). (10.9)

For M0 one may take B=4, and for M2, B=12/5.

Proof.

The first differences satisfy |qn|≤B and |q~n−qn|≤η. Orthogonality gives a tail bound B⁢rN+1/2⁢(1−r2) and a finite-noise bound at most η/2⁢(1−r2). Add them by the triangle inequality. ∎

The theorem controls a smoothed global kernel, not the error in a cusp derivative or a Stokes constant. Sending r↑1 removes smoothing and worsens the bound. Moreover, differences between floating-point discretizations are sensitivity tests, not a proved value of η; the numerical section does not use equation (10.9) to claim certified error bars.

11 Inverse reconstruction of trans-series sectors#

11.1 State the resurgent class before asserting uniqueness#

The exact transform of theorem 10.1 is unconditional in its stated functional or distributional sense. To interpret its pieces as trans-series sectors, additional analytic structure is required.

Fix an action spacing A>0 and a lateral continuation convention, denoted +. Assume that the physical inverse kernel has the locally finite representation

hphys⁢(t)=∑k≥0𝟏t>k⁢A⁢hk+⁢(t−k⁢A). (11.1)

Each hk is required to have a uniquely specified power–logarithmic germ at zero, to be analytically continuable along the chosen paths past subsequent thresholds, and to have growth permitting the corresponding Laplace transforms. We work in a fixed quasianalytic germ class, such as convergent power–log germs on a logarithmic cover; arbitrary additions flat at the germ origin are excluded. Distributional point contributions can be accommodated, but are not needed for the first-moment threshold analyzed below.

These are substantive assumptions. In particular, equation (11.1) is an exact decomposition, not an equality of formal asymptotic series. The known Wiener–Hopf trans-series provides the relevant sector structure for Lieb–Liniger [14]; a general proof of all its global continuation and summability properties directly from equation (7.1) is not supplied here.

Theorem 11.1 (Conditional triangular sector reconstruction).

Within the class just specified, the complete conformal coefficient sequence, the action spacing and the lateral convention determine every sector germ. Explicitly,

h0⁢(s) =hphys⁢(s), 0<s<A, (11.2)
hk⁢(s) =hphys⁢(k⁢A+s)−∑j=0k−1hj+⁢((k−j)⁢A+s), 0<s<A. (11.3)
Proof.

The coefficient inverse determines hphys. On the first interval only the zeroth sector is present, so its germ is known. Its analytic continuation along the prescribed path is unique. Suppose the first k germs and their prescribed continuations have been determined. On (k⁢A,(k+1)⁢A), subtracting those continued terms in equation (11.1) leaves exactly the translated kth germ. Induction gives existence of the reconstruction and uniqueness within the assumed class. ∎

In exact arithmetic, the continuation operation can be described by translating Taylor germs through overlapping disks along paths that avoid the singularities. In finite precision it can be severely ill-conditioned. The theorem identifies the inverse operation; it does not remove the analytic continuation problem or certify a finite-data algorithm for it.

For the auxiliary Lieb–Liniger moments, equation (9.7) gives A=π. At the second threshold, one must subtract both the continuation of h0 and that of h1. A peak at 2⁢π in a coefficient spectrum is not, by itself, the second-instanton amplitude.

11.2 From a sector germ to its fluctuation coefficients#

Suppose a reconstructed germ has terms

hk⁢(s)=∑m,rdk,m,r⁢sβm−1⁢(log⁡s)r,ℜ⁡βm>0. (11.4)

Then

ℒ⁢[sβ−1⁢(log⁡s)r]⁢(w)=∂βr{Γ⁢(β)⁢w−β}. (11.5)

Writing the corresponding term of the fluctuation series as ∑ℓck,m,ℓ⁢w−βm⁢(log⁡w)ℓ, we obtain the finite triangular coefficient map

ck,m,ℓ=(−1)ℓ∑r≥ℓ(rℓ)Γ(r−ℓ)(βm)dk,m,r. (11.6)

For the first nonperturbative sector of the smoothed moment, βm=m+2. In the log-free case,

ck,m,0=(m+1)!⁢dk,m,0. (11.7)

Thus h1⁢(s)=d0⁢s+d1⁢s2+d2⁢s3+⋯ gives e−π⁢w⁢(d0⁢w−2+2⁢d1⁢w−3+6⁢d2⁢w−4+⋯).

A local Mellin projection makes the extraction precise. Let

Jk⁢(λ)=∫0ϵsλ−1⁢hk⁢(s)⁢ds. (11.8)

The term in equation (11.4) gives the principal part

(−1)r⁢r!⁢dk,m,r(λ+βm−1)r+1. (11.9)

Changing the cutoff changes only the regular part at this pole. The inverse procedure has therefore returned to the same residues and finite parts that governed the elementary examples, but its global input is now the conformal coefficient sequence.

For the moments, the operations from {bn} to sector germs are linear once the action and continuation conventions are fixed, although they are not generally finite-support operations on the sequence. Undoing (w+1)−2 and reverting to physical coupling are subsequent nonlinear algebraic operations on the trans-series.

11.3 Stokes discontinuity versus an independent real sector#

Near the first threshold, suppose the real kernel has the local form

hphys⁢(A+s)=hreg⁢(s)+C⁢s⁢log⁡|s|+R⁢s++O⁢(s2⁢log2⁡|s|),s+=max⁡(s,0). (11.10)

The inherited perturbative singular germ is C⁢s⁢log⁡(−s). On the upper continuation, log⁡(−s)=log⁡s−i⁢π for s>0. Consequently,

Disc⁡h0⁢(A+s) =−2⁢π⁢i⁢C⁢s+⋯, (11.11)
Disc⁡H0⁢(w) =−2⁢π⁢i⁢C⁢e−A⁢w⁢w−2+⋯, (11.12)
h1+⁢(s) =(R+i⁢π⁢C)⁢s+⋯. (11.13)

The logarithmic coefficient fixes the discontinuity. The real one-sided term is an additional datum of the physical completion in this convention. To quote an abstract Stokes constant rather than an observable discontinuity, the normalization of the relevant sector must also be fixed.

Orthogonality and fixed-argument Laguerre asymptotics turn equation (11.10) into a direct coefficient signature:

qn(A)∼A3/421/4⁢πn−5/4[πCsinθn−Rcosθn],θn=22⁢A⁢n−π4. (11.14)

The derivation, including the signs, is given in appendix B. The phase is linear in n, which permits a windowed frequency scan. Higher power–log terms generate lower-order inverse-square-root and logarithmic corrections. Neglecting them produces phase leakage between the two quadratures, a visible limitation in the numerical test.

11.4 What the complete inverse does and does not identify#

Combining the maps gives

{en} →finite recursion/reversion{bn(0),bn(2)}→Laguerre inversehphys(0),hphys(2) (11.15)
→continued shifted subtraction{hk(0),hk(2)}→Mellin poles / gamma derivativesmoment trans-series
→physical-coupling reversionenergy trans-series.

The full sequence determines the selected physical observable. It determines its sector amplitudes in a fixed convention, not a unique separation between an arbitrarily normalized basis sector and a trans-series parameter. If several independent sectors have the same action and local exponent structure, one scalar observable generally determines only their combined contribution unless further normalization or observable data are supplied.

Nor can finitely many unrestricted coefficients determine a nonperturbative amplitude. For any N,

Δ⁢M⁢(a)=ε⁢aN+1⁢exp⁡[−A⁢1+a1−a] (11.16)

is holomorphic in the disk, leaves b0,…,bN unchanged, and changes the leading e−A⁢w amplitude by ε. It need not solve the fixed Lieb–Liniger equation. Its purpose is to show why structural information or a priori bounds, not just more elaborate fits to a finite prefix, are required for controlled inverse reconstruction.

12 Numerical tests: what is actually reconstructed#

The computation is designed to separate three questions: whether strong-origin coefficients reach weak coupling, whether their inverse kernel exposes the action lattice, and whether finite data determine amplitudes accurately. These are progressively harder tasks. The supplied code and data reproduce the tests below; no weak-coupling trans-series coefficients enter the generation of the conformal sequence.

12.1 Generation and independent checks#

The rational kernel in the conformal coordinate gives a polynomial recurrence requiring O⁢(N⁢M2) operations and O⁢(M2) working memory for N coefficients and M quadrature nodes. The recurrence is stated in appendix C. With sufficiently many Gauss–Legendre nodes, every polynomial integral required through the retained order is exact in exact arithmetic. The implementation uses ordinary floating point, so this algebraic observation is not an interval-arithmetic certification.

A fresh run generated orders 0 through 4,000 for both moments using 2,048 nodes. Against a separately generated 2,020-node dataset, the maximum absolute changes were 2.09×10−10 for the I0 coefficients and 4.78×10−11 for the I2 coefficients. The changes in the corresponding first differences were 6.53×10−13 and 3.61×10−13. The first differences, rather than the original coefficients, enter the inverse transform.

Additional tests evaluate the special-function identities at 60-decimal working precision, verify the first five Lang polynomials symbolically, and check the energy-to-moment conversion against directly generated coefficients. The suite includes an exactly solvable inverse problem with independently adjustable logarithmic and one-sided amplitudes; subappendix C.2 gives its formulas. None of these tests substitutes for a proof of finite-precision stability at all orders.

12.2 Convergent continuation to weak coupling#

Table 2 compares truncated conformal moment series with direct Nyström solutions of equation (7.1). The comparison is at fixed α: the table lists the physical γ of the reference solution. Thus it tests the parametric continuation, not a separate numerical reversion at fixed γ.

The rate is consistent with

a=e−arsinh⁡(α/2)∼e−α/2. (12.1)

At fixed accuracy one consequently expects a useful coefficient count of order 1/α, up to logarithmic factors and coefficient growth. The experiment confirms access to weak coupling; it does not distinguish exponentially small sectors by subtracting two weak-coupling evaluations.

12.3 Finding the actions without imposing their locations#

For the I0 data, form qn=(bn−bn−1)/2. A continuous scan fits the oscillatory signature in equation (11.14) over 0.5<A<16. The fit uses the orders from approximately 0.15⁢N to N, with a smooth window in n. A constant term absorbs part of the slowly varying background. The scan locates the peaks first; the lattice π⁢ℕ is used only for comparison in table 3.

12.4 The first logarithmic strength, and the unresolved quadrature#

After detecting the first action, set A=π and fit the leading two quadratures in equation (11.14). In the normalization of this paper, the auxiliary-moment trans-series of Ref. [14] gives

I0(1),+⁢(α)∼i2⁢e2⁢e−4⁢π/α,Cref=12⁢π⁢e2=0.0215392793018486⁢…,Rref=0. (12.2)

For clarity about the normalization, that reference writes the small-gap capacitance as Ccap=(ϵ0⁢π⁢r2/d)⁢[C(0)+δ⁢C(1)⁢e−2⁢(1/δ+1)+⋯], with δ=α/(2⁢π) and C(1)=2⁢i+O⁢(δ⁢log⁡δ). Since Ccap=2⁢ϵ0⁢r⁢I0 and d=α⁢r, its leading term becomes equation (12.2). The sign changes with lateral convention. This reference value is a benchmark, not an input to coefficient generation or action detection.

The numerical conclusion is deliberately limited. Five action locations are detected, and the first logarithmic/discontinuity strength is estimated at roughly the two-percent level. The real one-sided quadrature is still contaminated, higher fluctuation coefficients are unstable under changes of fitting window, and recursive subtraction through higher sectors has not been numerically validated. The formal inverse construction is stronger than this finite-data implementation.

13 Synthesis: where the information resides#

The coefficient connection has two complementary forms. In the elementary examples, a meromorphic moment function places the two coefficient systems on opposite sides of the same index plane. In Lieb–Liniger, a convergent conformal germ determines a causal inverse kernel, whose translated singular structure contains the weak-coupling sectors. Both descriptions separate local singular data from the global information needed to connect endpoints.

The exponential integral gives the cleanest dictionary: values of Γ⁢(v+1) at positive indices are factorials, residues at negative indices are reciprocal factorials, and finite parts are harmonic-number coefficients. The incomplete-gamma family shows why inverse-power Borel tails alone can miss an analytic sector. Airy shows how two nonresonant Mellin pole families yield two convergent local towers. Riccati shows that nonlinear transformations preserve an exact connection while changing convergence radii and introducing higher logarithmic powers; it also distinguishes the factorial branch from a different branch carrying a freely adjustable exponentially small parameter. The full-line Poisson problem demonstrates that the same Mellin mechanism extends beyond differential equations.

For finite-interval Lieb–Liniger, the endpoint is a boundary problem, not a single gamma-function identity. The analytic Fredholm argument proves a conformal domain in which the strong-origin moment series converges. The normalized kernel explains Lang’s denominator and polynomial-degree pattern without proving convergence of that separate regrouping. The Laguerre transform then gives an exact inverse kernel, and its Abel-regularized version has an explicit truncation/noise estimate. Under a fixed resurgent germ class and lateral convention, translated-support subtraction recovers all sector germs and gamma derivatives convert them into fluctuation coefficients.

The remaining analytic and numerical tasks are sharply delineated. One must derive the required exact sector class and continuation bounds directly from the finite-interval equation to remove the conditional hypothesis. One must also stabilize continuation and singularity extraction to convert the infinite-data inverse into a controlled finite-data reconstruction of higher coefficients. The smoothing estimate provides one ingredient, but it does not by itself bound a singular derivative. These are specific missing estimates, not missing definitions of the inverse map.

The central lesson can be stated without conflating uniqueness with stability:

The complete convergent coefficient sequence can encode a full trans-series, but the encoding is global. Mellin continuation or inverse-Laplace reconstruction makes the correspondence explicit; analytic class, contour convention and finite-data control determine what can actually be recovered.

Appendix A Positive densities for the master family and the Riccati branch#

A.1 The hypergeometric density#

For μ>0, 0<ν<1, Euler’s integral gives

F12⁢(μ,ν;1;−p)=1Γ⁢(ν)⁢Γ⁢(1−ν)⁢∫01vν−1⁢(1−v)−ν⁢(1+p⁢v)−μ⁢dv. (A.1)

Insert

(1+p⁢v)−μ=1Γ⁢(μ)⁢∫0∞tμ−1⁢v−μ⁢e−t/v⁢e−p⁢t⁢dt. (A.2)

All factors are nonnegative for positive real variables, so exchanging the integrals is justified by Tonelli’s theorem. The substitution v=(1+y)−1 in the remaining integral produces

ρμ,ν⁢(t)=tμ−1⁢e−tΓ⁢(μ)⁢Γ⁢(ν)⁢Γ⁢(1−ν)⁢∫0∞y−ν⁢(1+y)μ−1⁢e−t⁢y⁢dy. (A.3)

The integral representation of U proves equation (4.20). Equivalently, ρ is the density of the product of independent gamma and beta variables, with parameters μ and (ν,1−ν). Its Mellin moments therefore are

∫0∞tv⁢ρμ,ν⁢(t)⁢dt=Γ⁢(μ+v)⁢Γ⁢(ν+v)Γ⁢(μ)⁢Γ⁢(ν)⁢Γ⁢(1+v),ℜ⁡v>max⁡(−μ,−ν). (A.4)

Laplace transforming in t, and then in p, yields the Borel and Stieltjes representations. When ν=1−μ, U⁢(1−ν,1+μ−ν,t)=U⁢(μ,2⁢μ,t) and the reflection formula gives

ρμ,1−μ⁢(t)=sin⁡π⁢μπ⁢e−t⁢Φμ,1−μ⁢(t)t. (A.5)

Setting μ=1/6 proves the Airy self-representation.

A.2 No omitted poles in the Riccati density#

Put D⁢(z)=1−z⁢G⁢(z). The integral

D⁢(z)=∫0∞t⁢e−tz+t⁢dt (A.6)

has a strictly negative imaginary part when ℑ⁡z>0, a strictly positive one when ℑ⁡z<0, and is positive on the positive real axis. Thus D has no zero in the cut plane. The quotient f∗=G/D has no off-cut poles that could add discrete terms to its dispersion representation.

For z=−t+i0, write G=X−i⁢Y, with X=−e−t⁢Ei⁡(t) and Y=π⁢e−t. Then

ℑ⁡G1+t⁢G=ℑ⁡G|1+t⁢G|2,−1π⁢ℑ⁡(f∗⁢(−t+i0)−1)=ρR⁢(t). (A.7)

At infinity, the exponential-integral asymptotics imply f∗−1=O⁢(z−1) uniformly on the large cut-plane contours needed for the dispersion relation. At zero, f∗=O⁢(1+|log⁡z|), so the small circular indentation contributes O⁢(r⁢|log⁡r|) and vanishes. Cauchy’s formula therefore gives equation (5.4) with no subtraction constant and no extra residues.

The expansions equations (5.9) and (5.10) follow by inserting the large- and small-t expansions of Ei⁡(t). In particular, the density has an exponential moment for every rate smaller than one. Within positive measures with such a bound, all its moments uniquely determine its Laplace transform near zero and hence the measure. This moment uniqueness does not prohibit unrelated exponentially small additions outside that class or solutions on a different Riccati branch.

Appendix B From a threshold cusp to an oscillatory coefficient tail#

Orthogonality gives

qn=2⁢∫0∞h⁢(t)⁢e−t⁢Ln⁢(2⁢t)⁢dt (B.1)

when h∈L2, and by localization for the singular contribution considered here. For fixed t>0, the Laguerre asymptotic [16] is

e−t⁢Ln⁢(2⁢t)∼cos⁡(2⁢2⁢n⁢t−π/4)π⁢(2⁢n⁢t)1/4. (B.2)

Near t=A+s, linearize the phase as θn+ωn⁢s, where

θn=2⁢2⁢A⁢n−π4,ωn=2⁢nA. (B.3)

Localize with a smooth cutoff equal to one at s=0. The leading high-frequency transforms, with positive ω, are

∫ℝs⁢log⁡|s|⁢ei⁢ω⁢s⁢d⁢s∼−i⁢πω2,∫0∞s⁢ei⁢ω⁢s⁢ds∼−1ω2. (B.4)

They can be obtained by differentiating the transform of log⁡|s| and by exponential regularization, respectively. Smooth cutoff terms do not change these leading local singular contributions. Thus the cusp part of qn is

2π⁢(2⁢n⁢A)1/4⁢ωn2⁢[π⁢C⁢sin⁡θn−R⁢cos⁡θn], (B.5)

which is equation (11.14). Curvature of the phase, variation of the amplitude and higher local power–log terms give subleading corrections. Other thresholds add their own oscillations; endpoint structure at t=0 supplies a separate background. The formula should therefore be used as a local asymptotic component, not as an exact representation of the complete coefficient sequence.

Appendix C Coefficient generation, exact test problem and reproducibility#

C.1 A recurrence with only four history levels#

Let d=x−y. In the conformal coordinate,

αα2+d2=a⁢(1−a2)1+(d2−2)⁢a2+a4. (C.1)

Define v0⁢(x)=1, set all negative-index objects to zero, and for n≥1 let

Rn⁢(x,y) =vn−1⁢(y)−vn−3⁢(y)+(2−(x−y)2)⁢Rn−2⁢(x,y)−Rn−4⁢(x,y), (C.2)
vn⁢(x) =1π⁢∫−11Rn⁢(x,y)⁢dy, (C.3)
bn(j) =∫−11xj⁢vn⁢(x)⁢dx. (C.4)

These equations are the coefficient form of the integral equation, not an approximation to it. Multiplication by a⁢(1−a2) explains why only earlier vn enter, so no linear solve is required at each coefficient order. Evenness permits pairing positive and negative Gauss nodes. A circular buffer stores four Rn arrays and four vn vectors.

For n≥1, the degree of vn is at most n−1. All integrands needed for bn(0) and bn(2) through order N consequently have degree at most N+1. Gauss–Legendre quadrature with 2⁢M−1≥N+1 integrates these polynomials exactly in exact arithmetic. The implementation uses an even node count exceeding that requirement. Roundoff is still present and is checked by node-count changes and independent direct solves.

C.2 An exactly solvable inverse benchmark#

Choose A>0 and independent real constants C,R, and set

M⁢(w)=−C⁢e−A⁢w⁢Ei⁡(A⁢w)+R⁢e−A⁢w,H⁢(w)=M⁢(w)(w+1)2. (C.5)

Here M⁢(w) denotes the same function expressed in the half-plane coordinate, rather than its disk Taylor series. The principal-value inverse of e−A⁢w⁢Ei⁡(A⁢w) is −PV(t−A)−1. Convolution with t⁢e−t gives, with s=t−A,

h⁢(t)=−C⁢{1−e−t+s⁢e−s⁢[Ei⁡(−A)−Ei⁡(s)]}+R⁢𝟏s>0⁢s⁢e−s. (C.6)

In particular, its threshold form is exactly C⁢s⁢log⁡|s|+R⁢s+ plus a regular term and higher corrections. This tests the normalization and sign of both quadratures independently.

For a purely coefficient-based implementation, put e−A⁢w⁢Ei⁡(A⁢w)=∑n≥0fn⁢an with w=(1+a)/(1−a). The first-order differential equation gives

(n+1)⁢fn+1+(2⁢A−2⁢n)⁢fn+(n−1)⁢fn−1=rn, (C.7)

where f0=e−A⁢Ei⁡(A), f−1=0, r0=2, and rn=4⁢(−1)n for n≥1. Also,

[an]⁢e−A⁢w=e−A⁢[Ln⁢(2⁢A)−Ln−1⁢(2⁢A)],L−1=0. (C.8)

The same first-difference Laguerre inverse can therefore be tested without computing any numerical inverse Laplace integral.

With A=2.3, C=0.017 and R=0.011, the 4,000-order kernel agrees with the exact expression at nine sample points away from the threshold to a maximum absolute discrepancy of 1.08×10−5. The leading-quadrature fit gives C≃0.016881 and R≃0.012804. This deliberately imperfect recovery shows that the finite-order amplitude contamination seen in Lieb–Liniger is not, by itself, evidence against the exact inverse identity.

C.3 Contents of the reproducibility bundle#

The bundle contains the manuscript source, vector figures, two conformal coefficient datasets, machine-readable test outputs, and the following scripts. generate_coefficients.py implements equation (C.4); reconstruct.py performs the Laguerre inversion and action/strength fits; energy_to_moments.py checks the triangular physical-energy conversion; lang_blocks.py generates the exact regrouped polynomials; verify_special_functions.py tests the elementary identities and density formulas; test_inverse.py runs the exact benchmark; and make_figures.py regenerates the direct-solve comparisons and numerical figures.

The reported run used Python 3.13.5, NumPy 2.3.5, SciPy 1.17.0, SymPy 1.14.0 and mpmath 1.3.0. The README gives commands and dataset provenance. The code does not implement arbitrary-order stable analytic continuation of sector germs, certified Stokes extraction or a proof of the conditional hypotheses. Its reproducible scope is exactly the finite-data evidence reported above.
